Q116273823.summary: Cut into a small faceted piece of rock crystal, Christ hangs on a cross with a footrest, arms spread wide, flanked by the Virgin and Saint John, with a star and a crescent above the arms of the cross and Greek letters running down either side. Cut as an intaglio seal, it would have left a raised impression of the Crucifixion, a sign of its owner's faith. Its clarity and tiny scale make it an intimate Byzantine devotional object.
facts: The Met dates the seal broadly to the 9th–11th century and records it as rock crystal, about 2 cm high (accession 86.11.38, purchased 1886).
Q116273823.notes: The Greek letters were not read or verified.

vam:O352751.summary: Woven in red, cream, blue and green silk, this small, worn roundel shows a frontal figure with long hair and a halo, both arms raised in the ancient gesture of prayer, standing between two stylised trees. A border of floral motifs and small crosses runs round the edge. The V&A identifies the figure as Christ; it is a rare and delicate witness to Christian imagery on luxury silks of late-antique Egypt.
facts: Samite, a twill-woven silk, is thought to have originated in Sasanian Persia; Byzantine workshops adopted the technique, and it became one of the great luxury textiles of the period (V&A).
The roundel was given to the V&A by Robert Taylor in 1900; the museum dates it to about AD 500–700 and attributes it to Egypt.
vam:O352751.notes: The identification as Christ follows the V&A. The orans (praying) pose is more usual for saints, the Virgin or the deceased than for Christ, and no inscription or cross-nimbus confirms the identity, so it should be treated as uncertain.
